Specialized structure of neural population codes in parietal cortex outputs

Low-dimensional neural manifolds: Despite high extrinsic dimensionality, large-scale recordings reveal that population activity often lies on low-dimensional manifolds (e.g 10-20 latent dimension 13) whose geometry tracks latent task variables 14; top-down feedback can re-orient these manifolds within tens of milliseconds, supporting rapid remapping across behavioral contexts.. Methods like MARBLE capture local flow fields on the manifold, revealing that task switching corresponds to traversals along nearly orthogonal axes, minimizing interference. A 2025 study examines perceptual categorization in macaque visual cortex (Figure) 47. The study analyzes mixed selectivity and neural geometry (Figure). A 2026 preprint examines human hippocampal spatial representations (Figure). The preprint tests generalization across agents and gaze (Figure).

PFC representations

Encodes task rules in low-dimensional subspaces; rather than hard-switching between task-specific encodings, brains seem to implement low-rank perturbations of population activity (see Rule et al., 2020; Aevermann et al., 2023). This allows for flexible reuse of shared representational axes with minimal interference

During the delay of a sequence-reproduction task, activity in thousands of lateral-prefrontal neurons collapses into three nearly orthogonal, ring-shaped manifolds-one for each ordinal position-so that each item rotates within its own low-dimensional subspace without perturbing the others, revealing a factorised and flexible code for sequence working memory.

Same idea: subspace coding; spiking activity is restricted to a low-dimensional subspace of the full high-dimensional population space (1D for each neuron) 15

Mixed selectivity: Cellular computations for complexity

Optimally Structured Mixed Selectivity. A Normative Theory of Control in Neural Circuits

Non-linear mixed selectivity: some neurons (especially those in control and associative regions) exhibit nonlinear tuning to mixtures of features (e.g stimulus, context, rule, reward; for example, a neuron that only responds to "butterfly" when it is first in the sequence 15). Such mixed selectivity inflates representational dimensionality so that simple linear readouts can realize a combinatorial explosion of possible policies..

Prefrontal cortex temporally multiplexes slow and fast dynamics in value learning and memory

Coordinate transforms

head-direction, grid, and place codes, give low-distortion coordinate frames. Parietal circuits perform learned transforms between frames (retinal->gaze-centered->hand-centered), enabling fast sensorimotor compilation and generalization across effectors

Cognitive maps

Predictive model of an environment, whether spatial or non-spatial

Can refer to section 5 in "Predictive Representations" for this section

Cognitive maps in PFC; OFC as cognitive map of task space

Phenomena

Self-location cells

Grid cells

If Grid Cells are the Answer, What is the Question? A Review of Normative Grid Cell Theory

Cells in the entorhinal cortex that tessellate space into a hexagonal coordinate system

Hierarchical ring attractors; populations of grid cells organize as toroidal structures where two circular coordinates encode 2D position 22

Found in EC, primary input to HPC

Spatial and semantic codes remain largely segregated through entorhinal cortex and only converge in hippocampus

Place cells

Mark discrete, context-dependent locations and replay trajectories during rest

Include information on tasks and future states (SR)

Discovery of spatial view neurons in hippo in the 80s/90s suggested allocentric map learrning

Object-vector and boundary cells

Landmark-vector cells encode allocentric distance-direction vectors to salient objects

Boundary cells spike near environmental borders, supplying basis functions for path-planning

Remapping and abstraction. Partial map remapping can occur in < 1 s after context change, while hippocampal ensembles preserve topological continuity across morphed environments-evidence for graph-like rather than metric storage 23

Models

CSCG (Clone-Structured Cognitive Graph)

Allocates multiple "clone" states to the same sensory cue so that identical observations can belong to distinct sequential contexts

Learning splits/merges clones to minimise ambiguity, producing a higher-order transition graph that captures laps, routes, and task phases

Naturally explains splitter cells, lap-specific place fields, landmark-vector and boundary tuning, and rapid context-specific remapping

Supports probabilistic inference and flexible sequence generation; replay and prospective sweeping emerge from graph traversal

Successor Representation (SR)

Stores a matrix of discounted future-state occupancies under the current policy; rows correspond to predictive place fields, eigenvectors resemble grid cells

The eigenvectors of SRs resemble grid cell firing patterns, even recapitulating hexagonality under biologically plausible constraints

Tomov et al. (2021) tested whether humans use successor features (SFs) and generalized policy improvement (GPI) for cross-task transfer. Participants learned tasks sharing transition structures but differing in reward functions, then faced a novel task. Results showed "policy reuse" - participants favored training policies that performed better on the new task even when suboptimal, a key signature of GPI that couldn’t be explained by pure model-based or model-free approaches.

The influential Temporal Context Model 24 of episodic memory can be re-expressed in a manner that resembles learning of a SR, with a temporal context vector serving as an eligibility trace 25; the resulting model spans the continuum between the vanilla SR and full model-based search. The degree to which vanilla SR vs model-based search is being used is determined by a scalar context drift parameter 25

Can be learned with a TD-like eligibility trace, enabling rapid value recomputation when reward locations (or task representations in general) shift

Accounts for field skew opposite running direction, theta-sequence look-ahead, and grid-to-place transformations, but struggles with repeated cues because it assumes one latent state per observation

Proposed as a middleman between the two canonical extremes of RL (model-free and model-based); supports lightweight planning in reasonably in-distribution scenarios by caching transition dynamics

Fully model-based RL transcends the SR limitation where states that are not frequently visited under the policy (which the SR was learned with) are not fully accounted for

Evidence for non-spatial SR-like representations in HPC-EC activity

Much of the existing neuro work on SR-activity correspondences use the discrete SR; need to scale up to naturalistic experiments and expressive models

Hybrid view

DG/CA3 recurrent circuitry builds the CSCG-like higher-order graph; CA1/entorhinal layers can sum over that graph online to compute an SR when needed

Combines context separation (clones) with efficient predictive evaluation (SR), reconciling fast remapping with stable predictive fields

Predicts grid-cell eigenvectors arise from spectral decomposition of the clone graph, and that SR read-outs will shift when policy or context changes even if the underlying graph is unchanged

Provides a unified explanation for both rapid context switching and habitual value-based navigation, matching a wide range of hippocampal and entorhinal data

There isn’t (yet) a single, canonical "CSCG + SR" paper, but several papers lay out the two halves and then explicitly point to how they can be combined:

The original predictive-map work-Stachenfeld, Botvinick & Gershman’s "The hippocampus as a predictive map"-shows how CA3-like recurrence can learn a successor-representation that CA1 can read out for planning and value learning.

Gershman’s earlier temporal-context paper even sketches the circuit idea that CA3 provides an SR-like prediction that is compared against entorhinal sensory drive in CA1.

On the higher-order-graph side, George and colleagues introduced the clone-structured cognitive graph (CSCG) and emphasised that its latent-state graph naturally overcomes the one-state-per-cue limitation of SR while still allowing an SR-style matrix to be computed over the clones for evaluation. A computational model uses clone-structured cognitive graphs (Figure) 49. The model learns spatial structure from ambiguous observations (Figure).

The most explicit bridge is in the recent theory paper "Space is a Latent Sequence" (Raju & Guntupalli, 2024). They argue that a CSCG-like model is the underlying data structure and that an SR emerges as a summary statistic-essentially the "read-out" you get when you integrate future clone occupancy.

Taken together, these papers provide the ingredients of the hybrid view even though no single article packages it under that label: CA3/DG circuitry can implement a clone-structured, higher-order graph; CA1 (and downstream cortico-striatal targets) can pool over that graph to produce the familiar successor-representation used for prediction, value transfer and planning.

How a CSCG or SR could be learned in CA3

Review paper; ask o3 for full math and verify

Several works have learned SFs with biologically plausible learning rules. Two notable examples: learning SFs with STDP; shown to be equivalent to TD with an eligibility trace. Learning SFs with STDP and theta sweeps leads to place cells that mirror biological behavior (also showed dorsal-ventral hippocampal gradient of place field sizes matches gradient of discount factors over SFs)

The former shows that STDP mathematically implements temporal difference learning with an eligibility trace, where the eligibility trace is dynamically determined by the behavioral timescale T (states traversed slowly -> T=0 ; quickly, T=1)

During normal behavior, place cells fire at constant rates for  100ms when the animal is in each location. The relatively long duration means the network performs TD(0) updates - learning through bootstrapping where each weight update depends on the next state’s predicted value. This allows learning connections across behavioral timescales (seconds) using millisecond STDP windows.

During replay events, place cells fire precisely timed single spikes separated by  7ms intervals. These fast sequences correspond to TD(1)/Monte Carlo learning, which samples entire trajectories and averages the discounted state occupancies without bootstrapping.

Synaptic weights converge to the successor representation matrix, where each element wij represents the expected future occupancy of state j starting from state i. Learning predictive cognitive maps with spiking neurons during behavior and replays - PMC The network automatically handles the bias-variance tradeoff: replay-based learning provides quick initial learning with low bias, while behavioral learning provides stable convergence with low variance. A 2026 predictive-mapping study models subicular spatial responses (Figure) 48. The study compares the successor-feature model with recorded subicular responses (Figure).

This means the same STDP rule automatically switches between these learning modes based purely on timing, without needing separate eligibility trace mechanisms. The biological timescales naturally implement the algorithmic distinction between bootstrapped and sampled learning.

Replays can learn trajectories never directly experienced, enabling offline policy refinement and shortcut discovery. The framework naturally explains why replay frequency decreases in familiar environments - you need the low-bias Monte Carlo updates most when your initial estimates are poor.

This bridges three levels of analysis: STDP at the implementation level, TD(λ) at the algorithmic level, and predictive cognitive maps at the computational level.

Goal of the theta model is to make a biologically plausible model of HPC-EC that accounts for both path integration and sensory prediction 26

They model the HPC as a Helmholtz machine that uses theta rhythms to determine whether the model is in the "wake" (model learns to infer latents from sensory data) or "sleep" (model learns to generate sensory data from latents) phase; uses local learning rules and runs theta sweeps at 5-10Hz, both of which are biologically plausible

Recent work shows that place fields follow a 3D hyperbolic geometry instead of Euclidean geometry; this results in an exponential number of small place fields relative to large place fields, given the same number of neurons. This representation far outpaces the capacity of a linear alternative and naturally supports a multiscale, deformable representation that expands dynamically with exploration experience 27

Dynamically expands in proportion to time spent exploring the environment

Schemas (higher-order relational priors)

Schema-based active inference supports rapid generalization of experience and frontal cortical coding of abstract structure

By "schema" I mean an abstract, reusable model of relations among entities and events that the brain learns across many episodes and then uses as a prior when interpreting, storing, and retrieving new experiences. Classic examples are scripts like "restaurant" or "airport" (ordered subevents, role relations, typical contingencies), spatial layouts such as "grid-like apartment" or "four-way intersection," and task structures like "odor sequence -> choice -> outcome." Schemas speed learning (including one-shot assimilation), guide segmentation of continuous experience into events, bias attention toward expected relations, and provide scaffolds for recall and inference. In rodents, once a flavor-place "paired-associate" schema has formed, a single new pairing can be learned and consolidated rapidly; in humans, schematic knowledge boosts encoding of narrative details that fit the script. These effects place schemas squarely as priors over relational graphs-they encode expected node types (roles, states), edge types (temporal/causal/contingency links), and transition statistics that new data are fit into 29, 30. The graph model tests reuse of learned structure (Figure). The model illustrates hierarchical abstraction and planning (Figure).

Schema congruence typically enhances memory and accelerates systems consolidation (faster hippocampal->neocortical integration), while controlled novelty against a schema can also stand out and be remembered well-resolving the apparent "schema vs. novelty" paradox. Schemas also support transfer: a previously learned task graph enables rapid re-learning when surface features change, and they enable state inference when observations are ambiguous by supplying hidden-state structure. At retrieval, schemas supply organized cues that steer memory search and reconstruction, improving recall of story details when schema representations were strong at encoding 31, 32, 33.

Mechanistically, schemas emerge from interactions among medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC/vmPFC), hippocampus/entorhinal cortex, orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), and posterior-medial default-mode hubs (posterior cingulate/precuneus, angular gyrus, parahippocampal and retrosplenial cortex). The posterior-medial (PM) pathway supplies contextual/situational/relational structure; the anterior-temporal (AT) pathway supplies item/semantic structure; both converge in the hippocampus and interact bidirectionally with mPFC during learning and consolidation. Thalamic nucleus reuniens forms a key conduit coordinating hippocampal-prefrontal coupling, including during sleep and extinction 34, 35, 36, 33.

Human fMRI with naturalistic narratives shows that anterior mPFC carries schema representations (e.g., "restaurant" vs. "airport") whose strength at encoding predicts later recall of story details; during retrieval, a partly distinct network (including parahippocampal and angular gyrus) carries schematic information. This fits the view that mPFC provides a scaffold at encoding onto which hippocampus and posterior cortex bind specific content 33.

In the classic rodent paradigm, once a schema exists, new pairings become hippocampal-independent rapidly-yet hippocampus still supplies event-specific detail and prediction. Single-unit and imaging work shows both schema-like generalization (including "schema cells" in primate hippocampus) and detail-specific coding, often organized along the long axis (anterior = coarser/general; posterior = finer/detail) and interacting with mPFC during assimilation and replay 29, 37, 30.

OFC represents the latent state space of tasks-the abstract rules linking observations, hidden states, and outcomes. In rats, OFC ensembles develop schema representations that compress across superficially different problems, converging onto a low-dimensional code for shared task structure; OFC populations also encode value-based schemas and contextual states that guide retrieval. Recent causal work indicates OFC schema cells can form even when one hippocampal output (ventral subiculum) is inactivated, and may form faster when hippocampal output is suppressed during transfer-highlighting complementary (and sometimes competitive) roles across the circuit 38, 39, 40.

Across PFC and OFC, learning typically reduces representational dimensionality as populations align around task-relevant latent variables; in the OFC schema studies this appears as manifold compression and cross-problem alignment. More generally, prefrontal geometry supports abstraction-neural state spaces factorize rule-informative variables that generalize to novel instances, whereas hippocampal geometry tends to preserve specificity. In vmPFC, even value is coded along a curved manifold whose geometry predicts patterns of context-dependent "irrational" choice, emphasizing that schemas instantiate nonlinear priors over relational variables rather than simple axes 40, 41, 42, 43.

Under naturalistic viewing/listening, posterior medial cortex, mPFC, and superior frontal areas express schematic event patterns that generalize across subjects and across modalities; disrupting the temporal order of events weakens these schematic patterns, consistent with schemas encoding expected temporal relations among subevents 44.

Rodent and human work converge on: slow accrual of a schema in neocortex; accelerated assimilation of congruent information once the scaffold exists; mPFC engagement and gene-expression changes as schema-congruent material is encoded; and hippocampal-prefrontal coordination (via direct/entorhinal routes and nucleus reuniens) during encoding, replay, sleep, and retrieval. These dynamics reconcile complementary learning systems with schema-driven "fast" consolidation 45, 30, 35.

Schemas sit "above" cognitive maps: maps encode metric/topological relations within a context, while schemas encode classes of contexts and their typical transition/causal structure. Predictive representations like the successor representation (often linked to hippocampus/entorhinal) provide building blocks; PFC/OFC then recode these building blocks into abstract, policy-relevant state spaces (state abstractions) that are reusable across tasks-i.e., relational priors 46.
